articles.blurb: Anthropic's Threat Intelligence team has identified and disrupted several operations in the past several months where threat actors tried to use Claude for malicious activity. This report shares case studies from those operations and describes how malicious use of Claude has evolved since the company's previous threat reports. The report covers disruptions between December 2025 and August. None of the misuse cases involved the use of Claude Fable or Mythos-class models.

It beats SWE-1.7 and Grok 4.6 on both score and cost, matches GPT-5.6 Sol and Fable 5/5.1 at a fraction of their price, and comes within a few points of GPT-6 Astra at a quarter of the cost.

articles.headline: OpenCodeReview (GitHub Repo)
articles.blurb: Open Code Review is an AI-powered code review CLI tool. It originated as Alibaba Group's internal official AI code review assistant — over the past two years, it has served tens of thousands of developers and identified millions of code defects. It has been validated at massive scale. The agent can read full file contents, search the codebase, inspect other changed files for context, and produce deep reviews.

articles.headline: OpenAI launches GPT-Live-1 for full-duplex voice agents
articles.blurb: GPT-Live-1 is now available in the OpenAI API at $0.05 per minute. The model adds full-duplex speech, interruption handling, and 12 voice options. It can listen and speak at the same time, handle interruptions and acknowledgements as they happen, and keep conversations moving while performing deep reasoning or actions. The model can control tone, space, and style through the system prompt. Early tests report 80% fewer interruptions than with previous turn-based systems.

articles.headline: Why the world's best AI startups write bad prompts (& how to fix this)

Treating prompts like product and code, with modular sections for background, behavior, and output, can improve agent quality, reduce regressions, and lower costs.

articles.headline: The lifecycle of a sharded Postgres query
articles.blurb: This post follows the journey of a PostgreSQL query through all of the layers of a complex sharded system. It aims to help readers understand what goes into making a large-scale sharded PostgreSQL deployment appear to be a single server even when spanning thousands of servers. A real database has hundreds of tables - the example in the post keeps the schema simple with two tables spread across four shards.

The industry is seeing more knowledge-sharing sessions on how to use AI models cost-effectively. More and more companies are setting per-developer limits on AI usage.

The model layer could offer outcomes pricing, but it will have the same problems as the app layer. articles.blurb: Shopping ad CTRs are rising while impressions are falling across thousands of campaigns, with clicks relatively flat or slightly down. One hypothesis is that Google's AI Overviews are appearing on queries less likely to generate ad clicks, leaving Shopping ads for higher-intent searches. The data doesn't prove AI Overviews are causing the decline, but advertisers should look beyond CTR and track impressions, clicks, and overall traffic to understand whether performance is actually improving.

articles.headline: YouTube influencers have an AI audience: What millions of citation events reveal about influencer sponsorships
articles.blurb: Sponsored YouTube videos can extend their marketing value into AI search when the video is cited, especially through the description text that names the sponsor. The sponsor appeared in 40% of AI answers that cited a sponsored video, compared with 32.3% when the video was not cited, and the lift reached 1.35x on unbranded prompts. Brands should make specific description language part of influencer contracts and track YouTube citations for the prompts that matter to them, rather than treating sponsorship as a view-based channel alone. The opportunity is temporary because YouTube citation rates fell 43% within a month, so citation monitoring needs to be ongoing.

articles.headline: The Legacy Brand De-Aging Playbook
articles.blurb: Sometimes a brand's old identity becomes valuable again simply because the category around it moved. As dining shifted toward fast casual, delivery, and pricier meals, Chili's leaned into value, booths, and the Triple Dipper, and a format that once looked dated became the countertrend against expensive takeout. Barnes & Noble made a similar bet, handing individual stores control over what to stock and display instead of running every location identically, so each one behaves like a local bookstore again. Both bets worked because the brand stopped trying to outrun its category and let the category's shift make its old strengths relevant.

articles.headline: Don't recommend your most expensive option
articles.blurb: Increase sales by labeling a mid-priced product as “recommended” instead of your most expensive option. In eight experiments involving more than 6,200 participants, sales of a recommended cafe drink increased 58% when a pricier option was added, while sales were unchanged without the recommendation. Consumers appear more receptive to recommendations when the suggested product is cheaper because the brand seems less motivated by profit. Use objective badges such as “Bestseller” when recommending a premium product, and test this pricing tactic on comparable products where customers can easily evaluate the price difference.

articles.headline: Google launches tool to check whether ads actually increase sales
articles.blurb: Google released an open-source tool that tests whether an ad actually caused a sale, not just which platform claims credit for one. GeoX works by comparing regions where a campaign keeps running against regions where it's paused or given more budget, then measuring how sales in each group differ from what historical data would have predicted anyway. It can track spend across platforms beyond Google's own and combine online and offline sales in the same test. It plugs into Google's existing Meridian measurement software, so the results can also refine how a budget gets split across channels.

articles.headline: Amazon gives OpenAI's ad business a boost, letting its advertisers into ChatGPT
articles.blurb: Amazon has spent months locking AI shopping agents like Claude and Gemini out of its own storefront while building its own AI shopping tools, then quietly became ChatGPT's top retail advertiser between April and August instead. It's now opening that same access to other brands that already buy through its demand-side platform, letting them run ads inside ChatGPT conversations too. Campaigns are still set up and managed inside Amazon's own systems, while OpenAI's ad system keeps control over which ad actually gets served.

articles.headline: AI, tools and transformation
articles.blurb: AI will not eliminate software so much as change how companies decide what gets automated, standardized, or left improvised. Most employees do not naturally identify the workflows that should become software, and important processes often span multiple teams and systems, so successful automation still requires people who can spot problems, design solutions, and get the organization to adopt them. AI will expand existing software and make tools like spreadsheets, email, and chatbots more capable, while also creating new vertical applications that move work between improvised and institutionalized systems. The bigger opportunity for businesses is to look beyond faster versions of existing workflows and identify new products, services, and operating models that AI makes possible for the first time.

articles.headline: Some companies are using ads to influence AI agents
articles.blurb: Time magazine is testing ads designed specifically for AI agents, exposing them to brand-verified facts before they access webpages. The goal is to influence what AI systems retain and potentially correct inaccurate information about brands. As agentic traffic grows, companies are also optimizing websites and product data for AI discovery and recommendations. Brands are beginning to treat AI agents as an emerging advertising and distribution channel.

articles.headline: How Starface Made Pimple Patches Cool
articles.blurb: Skincare spent decades built around the idea that a good product should be invisible. Starface inverted that by making a pimple patch impossible to miss, then expanded through Target, Walmart, Sephora, and Ulta specifically because its bright yellow stars stand out against a retail aisle of clinical whites and pastels. That same bet is now showing up industry-wide, with LED light masks and other visible skincare wearables replacing creams that disappear on the skin.

The move would give Block a federal framework for certain digital asset activities and adds it to a growing group of fintech and crypto companies seeking national bank charters.

articles.headline: Chime agrees to acquire Stride Bank for $590M
articles.blurb: Chime agreed to acquire longtime partner Stride Bank for $590 million in cash, giving the fintech a national bank charter and bringing banking infrastructure in-house under the future Chime Bank, N.A. The deal is expected to be immediately accretive and generate more than $100 million in net synergies through lower partner-bank fees, cheaper funding, and expanded lending, while giving Chime tighter control over product development, compliance, and its balance sheet.

articles.headline: PayPal helps developers build application-specific PYUSD-backed stablecoins
articles.blurb: PayPal is working with crypto specialists MoonPay and M0 on an infrastructure platform that lets developers create application-specific stablecoins backed by PYUSD. Launched in 2023, PYUSD is PayPal's own dollar-backed stablecoin, issued by Paxos Trust Company, a federally regulated national banking association. The new platform, called PYUSDx, aims to help developers launch application-specific stablecoins quickly while leveraging the core foundation of PayPal's established token.

articles.headline: Data center spending to reach $32T by 2050, PwC says
articles.blurb: PwC projects that meeting global demand for artificial intelligence will require $31.6 trillion in infrastructure investment through 2050, potentially rising to $50 trillion if adoption accelerates. The US is expected to capture nearly half of the capital, while recurring replacements of chips and other hardware will account for most of the investment. Access to reliable electricity and semiconductors will ultimately determine which regions benefit most.

articles.headline: DeFi: Robinhood's leading launchpad stapled $5B of memes to stocks

The structure mirrors Olympus DAO's 2021 bonding trick, using real equity exposure as collateral to give meme coins a quoted price, with one case pushing a wrapped HIMS token to $132 versus a $28 real close.

articles.blurb: ION announced that Coinbase selected its XTP for Event Contracts platform to support clearing and back-office processing for Kalshi's prediction market contracts. The partnership gives Coinbase real-time infrastructure for contract creation, resolution, settlement, high-volume onboarding, and 24/7 automated processing, with XTP already supporting Kalshi's first one million Super Bowl weekend trades.

articles.headline: Visa brings onchain lending into everyday payments
articles.blurb: Visa is combining VisaNet settlement data with blockchain lending infrastructure to help stablecoin-linked card programs and fintechs access working capital, using real-time payment performance to support underwriting, collateral management, and automated repayment. The model is already live with Credit Coop, which has financed more than $2.5 billion of settlement volume with zero defaults, as Visa expands its broader stablecoin strategy across settlement, card programs, and digital asset infrastructure.

articles.headline: After $240M bitcoin theft, crypto scammers' spending spree comes to an end
articles.blurb: A group of young hackers allegedly stole more than 4,100 bitcoin by impersonating Google and Gemini representatives and manipulating a wealthy investor into revealing his security codes. Their extravagant purchases, including luxury cars, private jets, mansions and a $569,000 night out, helped attract attention before investigators traced the scheme through an exposed IP address. Eighteen people have been charged, with alleged ringleader Malone Lam expected to become the eleventh to plead guilty.

articles.headline: Split Pay raises $125M to bring net-30 financing to rent
articles.blurb: Split Pay raised $125 million from Khosla Ventures, Thrive Capital, and Max Levchin to let renters defer up to half of a bill for 30 days, charging 2% of the full bill plus $10 per month with no interest or late fees. The bigger bet is underwriting: Split Pay says its non-FICO model uses 50,000 variables and has achieved a 97.5% repayment rate across $350 million of originations, using rent as a high-frequency wedge to build a richer cash-flow dataset and eventually expand into broader consumer credit.

Microsoft says artificial intelligence is helping to speed the discovery of vulnerabilities, but security experts warn that many organizations already are struggling to prioritize the more human-intensive endeavor of testing and deploying so many fixes each month.

articles.headline: FBI Probes Service Selling 153M+ Drivers Licenses
articles.blurb: A new identity theft service launched on the dark web this week is selling digital scans of more than 153 million drivers licenses from people in the United States and Canada. Based on interviews with individuals whose licenses are available for purchase on this service, it appears to be siphoning images collected by a widely-used identity verification company based in Louisiana. KrebsOnSecurity also has learned that the New Orleans field office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) today launched an official inquiry into the source of the images.

articles.headline: Two Alleged ‘TeamPCP’ Hackers Arrested in Australia
articles.blurb: Authorities in Australia have arrested two men believed to be members of TeamPCP, a prolific cybercrime and data extortion group blamed for perpetrating the longest running spree of software supply chain attacks ever. In a statement released today, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) said two unnamed suspects from Western Australia, aged 21 and 23, were arrested in connection with a "sophisticated cybercrime syndicate that allegedly created malicious open-source software to rob thousands of global businesses." The AFP did not name the defendants, but KrebsOnSecurity learned the 21-year-old suspect's real identity in June, and has been communicating with him ever since. This story includes interviews with TeamPCP's self-described spokesperson, and examines clues left behind by the TeamPCP leader that likely led to his undoing.

articles.headline: Who’s Tracking You? Use This New Service to Find Out
articles.blurb: It can be daunting to determine who's responsible for showing ads on the websites we visit, or who's harvesting data from the mobile apps we use every day.
